name: AKU contributes to first international standards to assess fetal growth and newborn size worldwide

content.text: "Healthcare practitioners already have WHO international growth standards for children from birth up to the age of 5 that are used in 140 countries worldwide. Now they will have international standards for the developing fetus and newborn too", explained José Villar, lead author and Professor of Perinatal Medicine at the Nuffield Department of Obstetrics & Gynaecology, University of Oxford in the UK.

Currently, fetal growth and newborn size are evaluated around the world using over 100 different locally produced growth charts.  They describe only how children grew in a particular population or region at a given time, rather than how a baby in the womb should grow when mothers have adequate health, nutrition, and socioeconomic status: the new international standards correct this situation.

"These new standards and standardized methods for comparing length/height and head circumference for gestational age are the best ways to compare populations across the globe," said Professor Zulfiqar Bhutta from AKU's Centre for Excellence in Women and Child Health in Karachi. "We hope their widespread use, in combination with the existing WHO Child Standards, will contribute to improved birth outcomes and reduced perinatal mortality and morbidity worldwide."

The INTERGROWTH 21st Project collected growth and size data, using the same equipment and methods, from eight diverse populations of babies born to 4607 healthy, well-nourished women in selected urban areas in Brazil, China, India, Italy, Kenya, Oman, the UK, and the USA. Women were selected based on an ideal environment for healthy growth, such as adequate nutrition, education, low environmental contaminants, and good healthcare.

To generate the first international standards for fetal growth, ultrasound scans were performed every 5 weeks from early pregnancy (14 weeks) to delivery to assess five growth measures using identical machines and measures in all countries.

In the second complementary study, new international centiles for weight, length, and head circumference for babies born between 33 and 42 weeks' gestation were obtained from more than 20,000 deliveries to healthy mothers selected using identical criteria as in the fetal growth study.  The measurements were obtained within 12 hours of birth by centrally trained teams using identical equipment in all countries.

According to Professor Villar, "From now on, international standards can be used worldwide to make judgements on growth and size from conception to 5 years." This would allow doctors, nurses and mid-wives to check growth from all the way from a mother's womb to school.

The INTERGROWTH 21st Lancet papers follow two recent landmark publications from the same group: the first showed that most of the variation in the size of babies born worldwide is due to socioeconomic, healthcare and nutritional differences rather than ethnicity or country of birth (Lancet Diabetes & Endocrinology, July 4); and the second described a new international standard for dating pregnancy by ultrasound during the first trimester (Ultrasound in Obstetrics & Gynecology, July 8).

content.title: AKU contributes to first international standards to assess fetal growth and newborn size worldwide
content.author: volunteer.pa
content.description: First international standards to access fetal growth and newborn size worldwide emerged from INTERGROWTH 21st, a collaborative effort of over 300 clinicians and researchers from 27 institutions across the world, including the Aga Khan University. They present the first international standards to assess fetal growth and newborn size worldwide in The Lancet. The six-year landmark project was funded by the Bill & Melinda Gates Foundation.
